Read IN FULL: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev/646bc8ac-afb6-41b4-8d24-dcbaf28144cd/scratchpad/turns_chunk04.txt

This file contains every user turn Marcel Navarro typed across ~49 Claude Code sessions while working as FED Lead on the Zimmermann PWA Kit (a Salesforce PWA Kit / React / Chakra codebase). Sessions are separated by `====` lines with a `### [tag] [date] Title — N user turns` header. Turns are marked `--- turn N ---`.

READ THE WHOLE FILE. It is large (~523,000 tokens), so read it in sequential slices using Read with offset/limit. Maintain a running findings list as you go and DISCARD raw text after each slice — never try to hold the whole file in context.

We are designing personal workflow skills for Marcel. The transcripts are the evidence for WHY those skills are needed. Extract these six things:

**1. RECURRING CORRECTIONS — the highest priority.**
Places where Marcel had to re-state an established way of working that had been ignored or got wrong. He has said he had to "stress again and again" the set approach. Find those. For each, give: verbatim quote (trimmed to the relevant sentences), the session title, turn number, and tag it with the area:
`overriding` | `tokens` | `components` | `atomic-design` (atoms/molecules/organisms) | `css-structure` | `css-strategy` | `tests` | `stories` | `a11y` | `typescript` | `contentful` | `scope` | `git/branching` | `other`
Count how many DISTINCT times each area comes up. That count is the single most important output.

**2. DESIGN CONFORMANCE.**
Where he had to check or re-check that a build matched the Figma design — variants, states, tokens, viewports, spacing. Quote the checks he actually performs and what he looks for.

**3. FRUSTRATION / RE-WORK SIGNALS.**
Turns containing corrections: "again", "I said", "no —", "that's not", "you missed", "why did you", "revert", "you were supposed to", "as I mentioned". These mark where the workflow broke down. Quote and categorise.

**4. WHAT WORKED.**
Successes. Especially any use of a closed-loop / multi-agent / orchestrator-builder-tester-scorer workflow. Quote how he set it up and what he said about the result. Also note any prompt pattern he reused because it worked.

**5. HIS PROMPT FORMULAS.**
Recurring phrasings and structures he types — the shape of his asks. We want to encode his voice and method into skills, so capture the actual language, not a paraphrase.

**6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR.**
He is also senior dev / reviewer. Where he reviews others' PRs or code, capture: what he checks, in what order, what he rejects, and how he phrases feedback.

OUTPUT: a structured report with these six sections. Lead section 1 with a frequency table of areas. Use verbatim quotes throughout — quotes are the deliverable, not summaries. Be concrete. If a section has nothing, say so explicitly.

9	---
10	## Role
11	You generate Zephyr Scale test cases from Jira requirements and upload them as
12	**drafts for human review**. You are the first pass, not the final word. A QA
13	engineer reviews everything you produce in the Zephyr UI before it becomes real.
14	## Constants
15	| Setting | Value |
16	|---|---|
17	| Jira site | `zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net` |
18	| Project key | `SFCC` |
19	| Target folder | `/Staging/<JIRA-KEY>` |
20	| Status on write | `Draft` — never anything else |
21	| Upload script | `~/tools/zephyr/zephyr-upload.ts` |
22	| Token | `$ZEPHYR_TOKEN` from Keychain — never read, print, or log it |
23	---
24	## Procedure
25	### 1. Read the requirement
26	Via the Atlassian MCP, fetch the Jira issue: summary, description, acceptance
27	criteria, issue type, status, **and comments**. Requirements frequently live in
28	comments rather than the description — read them.
29	Follow every linked Confluence page and read it. If a link is dead or you lack
30	access, say so explicitly rather than proceeding on partial information.
31	### 2. Assess before generating
32	Report to the user, before writing anything:
33	- How many distinct acceptance criteria you found
34	- Anything ambiguous, contradictory, or underspecified
35	- Anything referenced but unreadable
36	**If acceptance criteria are ambiguous, stop and ask.** Do not resolve ambiguity
37	by picking the most plausible reading. A confidently-worded test case built on a
38	guess is worse than no test case, because it passes review by looking right.
39	### 3. Generate
40	One test case per acceptance criterion, plus error and edge paths **that the
41	requirement actually states**. Do not invent requirements to reach a target count.
42	Naming: `<Feature>: <behaviour being verified>`
43	e.g. `Checkout: rejects expired payment method`
44	Each case gets:
45	- `name` — as above, unique within the project
46	- `objective` — one sentence, what this proves
47	- `precondition` — required state, or omit
48	- `folder` — `/Staging/<JIRA-KEY>`

3314	## Requirements for every output
3315	
3316	- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
3317	- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
3318	- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.

3324	## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)
3325	
3326	openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
3327	formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
3328	`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.
3329	
3330	```bash
3331	python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
3332	```
3333	
3334	LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
3335	`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
3336	`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
3337	withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
3338	again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
3339	only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
3340	workbook.
3341	
3342	**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
3343	range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
3344	Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.
3345	
3346	**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
3347	then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$Banalyze` — the `[1]` is an index
3348	into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
3349	That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
3350	data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
3351	real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
3352	— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
3353	and accepts the loss).

3355	## Choosing formulas that survive verification
3356	
3357	LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
3358	literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.
3359	
3360	- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
3361	- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.
3362	- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value — and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.
3363	- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** — a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.
3364	
3365	## openpyxl gotchas
3366	
3367	- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.
3368	- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal — permanently.
3369	- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** — run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `""` also reads back as `None`.)
3370	- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.
3371	- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.
3372	- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$Bfile`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

FOUND at 10858
meeting 2 notes:

"Based on the transcribed meeting discussion.
FED Executive Takeaway
The strongest message from Tim was:
Stop thinking about pages as primary deliverables and think about reusable, configurable components as the primary deliverables.
The homepage, cart, PDP/PLP experiences, etc. should largely become assemblies of previously built components, not separate frontend implementations.
For FED, this means:
Component completeness is critical.
Variant support must be designed upfront.
Contentful configuration drives rendering.
Page stories should primarily validate composition and integration, not rebuild functionality.
What Matters Most for FED
1. Components Must Support All Variants
The editorial card example was used repeatedly.
The expectation is that a FED developer building a component should account for:
text alignment variants
CTA visibility variants
title visibility variants
body copy variants
layout variants
before the component is considered complete.
FED Implication
Avoid:
Homepage Editorial Card
PLP Editorial Card
Landing Page Editorial Card
Instead:
One Editorial Card component + all supported variants
The page determines configuration.
The component owns behavior.
2. FED Stories Should Focus on Rendering Behavior
There was a clear separation made between:
Contentful Stories
Responsible for:
content model fields
editorial configuration
required/optional fields
authoring controls
FED / PWA Stories
Responsible for:
rendering
responsiveness
accessibility
link behavior
user interactions
component state handling
This is actually useful from a backlog standpoint because it removes duplication between Contentful and FED work.
Potential FED Story Pattern
Instead of:
Build Editorial Card
Think:
Render Editorial Card content model according to Figma specifications across all supported configurations.
3. Accessibility Requirements Need To Be Explicit
One specific implementation point surfaced.
For image alt text:
If alt text exists → render it.
If alt text does not exist → do not render the attribute.
For FED this means:
accessibility behavior should be documented directly in ACs
don't assume CMS fields are always populated
frontend rendering needs to account for missing content safely
4. Homepage Tickets Are Probably Over-Scoped
A major discussion point was:
"What actually belongs in a Homepage Epic?"
The consensus was essentially:
The homepage is mostly:
Hero
Editorial modules
Category modules
Content modules
Promotional modules
all assembled together.
If those components already exist, there shouldn't be significant additional frontend implementation.
FED Impact
When sizing homepage work:
Separate:
Component Build
real FED effort
from
Page Composition
assembly/configuration effort
integration testing
visual validation
Those should not be estimated the same way.
5. Component Validation Should Happen Early
Tim described an iterative approach where components are progressively dropped into a working homepage as they're completed.
Rather than:
Build everything
Then build homepage
Then test homepage
the idea is:
Build component
Drop component into page
Verify rendering
Repeat
FED Impact
This aligns well with:
Storybook
Preview environments
Contentful preview workflows
Incremental QA
Potentially less big-bang integration risk later.
6. Page-Level Testing Still Belongs To FED
Even though pages aren't primary development units anymore, the meeting did reinforce that pages still need validation.
Specifically:
spacing
layout
design fidelity
responsive behavior
assembled user experience
Once the page is composed, someone still needs to verify that it matches design expectations.
FED Ownership Area
I would expect FED to remain heavily involved in:
visual QA
responsive QA
integration validation
design parity verification
even if the page itself isn't a dedicated implementation story.
Areas Where FED Should Push Back / Ask Questions
Recommendation Components
The cart example exposed some unclear requirements around:
Recommended For You
Shop The Look
Complete The Look
Questions raised included:
Manual curation?
Product relationships?
Behavioural/personalized recommendations?
Cookie-dependent experiences?
The group did not resolve this.
FED Risk
Frontend implementation differs significantly depending on:
static curated content
SFCC-driven recommendations
Einstein recommendations
personalization engines
Before sizing work, FED should ensure ownership and data source are clarified.
External Link Handling
There was uncertainty around:
external links
opening new tabs
security-related link attributes
No final decision was reached.
FED Follow-Up Needed
Before component implementation begins, confirm the desired standard for:
external links
internal links
new-tab behavior
Otherwise multiple developers may implement differently.

   > *"but before we focus into the code, let's look into the JIRA ticket / user story first so we can take note of the user story: it's requirements, ACs, description, **separation of concerns, scope**, etc. in-depth and full-on"* — PR #70, t3
2. **Requirements → design → code, in parallel agents.** (PR #57, t3–t8: Jira / branch state / PR review state / Figma spec.)
3. **Audit against the codebase's own rules, not general taste.**
   > *"ensure the audit is **primarily rooted in the codebase docs/cicd/rules/standards/conventions**"* — 07-28, t7
   > *"grounded by the facts in the codebase: rules, standards, conventions, the cicd, coderabbit config"* — t12/t13
4. **Assume intent before assuming bug.**
   > *"**when a change is flagged, look into the case where it could possible be intentional or an actual bug/missed aspect**"* — 07-28, t6/t7
5. **Triage findings by value, not by count.**
   > *"**which of these findings are cosmetic and do not bring actual value to the code?**"* — t8
   > *"do these findings bring actual value or are some just cosmetic? **perhaps we should categorize the findings in that manner?**"* — t9
6. **Force re-verification of every finding.**
   > *"**re-verify and re-trace all findings - if you flagged them, there must be a valid reason behind it**"* — t10
   > *"all our findings are backed by checking and testing, correct? and we have utmost confidence in them?"* — PR #70, t11
7. **Cross-check against CodeRabbit, then look for conflicts and for contamination.** (see §4)
8. **Weigh authorship, but don't let it change the verdict.**
   > *"additional context: **it's the Integration Lead who did this PR - does that change anything?**"* — t25 and again t45
   > *"take these into consideration: **the proposal is by Tim, the lead architect and i'm Tier 1 - what does that change**"* — ZIMM - Tag, t33
9. **Size the remediation before deciding.**
   > *"how big of a refactor is needed to fix this concern?"* (t20, t22, t41) → *"how big of a refactor is needed to fix **all** the concerns?"* (t42)
   > *"provide me a simple to understand example of what blocker #1's use-case is and what the problem with it is?"* (t19, t21, t43)
   > *"what's the difference between the current coded implementation and how it should be?"* (t18, t44)
   > *"what's the connection of blocker #2 to blocker #1? if blocker #1 gets resolved? are they to be fixed together?"* (t23)
10. **Then write the comment, then the Teams heads-up.**

### The verdict framing he always asks for

> **"report back with a verdict if to approve or request changes"** — used in essentially every PR session (07-20 t1/t4, 07-28 t3/t4/t6/t7/t11/t12/t13/t36, PR #70 t6).
> Also: *"perform another complete/deep check/audit - **the Tier-1 Approvers are unsure of this PR**"* and *"do another audit across all 3 PRs to **challenge, confirm, and validate** the verdicts"* (07-20, t2/t6) — and when a re-run flipped the verdict he interrogated the flip: *"what was the difference with the previous and this new review pass? why was it given the go-signal on the previous and changes requested on this recent review pass?"* (t3).

### What he rejects

- **Rewriting OOTB instead of overriding it** — *"why does the code in this PR #57, change the entire out-of-the-box PDP page? can't we override and then ship only the components without having to remove the other parts that are out-of-the-box that haven't been custom built yet?"*
- **Code with no design or ticket behind it** — *"the breadcrumb, where is that taken from? i didn't see it in the figma designs? is it specified in the ticket?"*
- **Scope creep dressed as thoroughness** — *"why are there so much e2e related code in here? … is that a lack in the footer code or overengineering and reaching for this PR?"*
- **Literal/absolute values instead of tokens** — *"first, why do we have literal/absolute values in these 4 files changed?"*
- **Non-conforming PR titles/bodies, and any Claude/CodeRabbit fingerprints** — *"remove claude mentions, coderabbit, and other irrelevant parts of the PR description/body"*; *"remove: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8"*
- **Unresolved review threads left open** — *"why did you leave a comment open? as an action item, this PR will not get resolved then"*
- **Secrets reaching the browser bundle** — the CPA-token finding on PR #41.
- **Cosmetic findings presented at the same weight as real ones.**
- **Findings that are only technically true** — *"are these being flagged as out of scope because of technicalities… or is it because they are genuinely and totally not usable"*

### How he phrases feedback — his actual sent message

> *"Hey Mani! Did a review pass on #41 (Contentful Preview), had to mark it request changes, heads up. Mostly small cleanups, but one bit genuinely needs your call:
>  The preview (CPA) token is ending up in the browser bundle, which runs against our own Contentful integration doc (§3/§4/§9 - preview token stays server-side / proxied via MRT). Since you own both the code and that doc: is client-side preview a deliberate call (→ we update the doc + gate it to non-prod), or do you want to proxy the draft fetch so the token stays server-side?
>  Also ran a full CodeRabbit pass to double-check, same core findings, and it also landed on request changes, **so it's not just me aha**. Full write-up's in the PR review."*
> — Check local branch status against remote (07-28), t56

The template he asked for explicitly:
> *"create a comment i could post/paste along as i put down my review of 'request changes' - **in the tone of: 'here's my review... i also ran a CodeRabbit review to verify and the same findings we're surfaced but its findings are/were...'**"* — t33

And the feedback-writing standard he set for himself:
> *"i first did a **feasibility check into the findings, tested and validated them** to ensure accuracy and appropriateness, once confirmed i wrote comments, **general and inline** - and wrote them in **natural language without sacrificing the technical accuracy** and aspect of the review findings"* — PR #70, t8

Observed pattern: friendly opener → the verdict up front → separate "small cleanups" from "the one thing that needs your call" → frame the blocker as a **question about intent**, citing the project's own doc by section → name the two acceptable resolutions → cite the independent tool as corroboration → self-deprecating softener → point to the full write-up. He always drafts a **short Teams message** to the author separately from the GitHub review, and a separate **"brief report to send to Tim"** for the lead.
